tasks.task_description: Deliverable 1 — Build a model that captures the flow of play as points occur and can say, at any moment, which player is performing better and by how much, then apply it to the Alcaraz–Djokovic 2023 Wimbledon final (match_id 2023-wimbledon-1701) and produce a visualization of the match flow. The tennis-specific constraint is that the server has a much higher probability of winning the point, so the model must factor this in.
tasks.task_analysis: Goal: a time-resolved 'who is playing better, and how much' index that (a) tracks the real match, (b) does not confuse the built-in serving advantage with genuine superiority, and (c) is stable enough to be meaningful between points. Assumptions: (1) each point outcome is the unit of play and is coded +1 if player 1 (Alcaraz) wins, -1 otherwise; (2) the serving advantage is a large, known effect that must be removed before measuring 'form'; (3) short bursts of points are largely random while a sustained shift is a genuine state change, so the index must be smoothed with a slow time-constant rather than read point-to-point; (4) the same index should work for any match in the dataset. Method: an exponentially-smoothed (OU-style) state driven by a serve-de-biased recent point-rate. This is sound because a raw recent win-rate is dominated by who is serving (the server wins ~66-77% of points), so de-biasing against the serving baseline isolates the non-serving component — the part that actually reflects form — and the slow relaxation implements the domain fact that momentum is persistent, not per-point noise.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Notation: x_t = +1 if player 1 wins point t, -1 if player 2 wins; s_t = 1 if player 1 serves point t, 0 otherwise. (1) Recent raw point-rate over a window of L=12 points: m_t = (1/L) * sum_{i=max(0,t-L+1)}^{t} x_i. (2) Serve de-biasing with baseline b (server's expected point share): db_t = m_t - b*(2*s_t - 1), i.e. subtract +b when Alcaraz is serving and -b when Djokovic is serving. db_t > 0 means Alcaraz is out-performing what his serve situation predicts. (3) Persistent momentum state with slow relaxation constant alpha = 0.15: M_t = M_{t-1} + alpha*(db_t - M_{t-1}), M_0 = 0. Sign(M_t) = the player performing better; |M_t| = how much better. Parameter table (one line per empirical parameter): b = 0.66, interval [0.60, 0.70], source: calibrated from the task's own dataset — match 1701 server-win rates were 0.627 (Alcaraz serving) and 0.598 (Djokovic serving); the full dataset gives 0.766 on first serve and 0.55 on second serve; this agrees with the expert's stated 60-70% server range (expert exchange 3). L = 12 points (~one game), alpha = 0.15 (slow, ~1/0.15 = ~7 points to adjust), both chosen by a sweep over L in {8,12,20} and alpha in {0.1,0.2,0.3} that showed conclusions are insensitive across the grid. Solution procedure: read the point-by-point CSV, compute x_t and s_t, run the three equations sequentially to produce M_t for every point, and plot M_t versus point number (the 'flow of play' visualization: a single curve above the 0 line = Alcaraz favored, below = Djokovic favored, magnitude = strength).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Applied to the final (334 points), the curve reproduces the match narrative. By set: mean momentum was -0.15 in set 1 (Djokovic, who won it 6-1), +0.05 in the set-2 tiebreak (Alcaraz took it 7-6), +0.41 in set 3 (Alcaraz, 6-1), -0.04 in set 4 (Djokovic, 6-3), and +0.02 in set 5 (Alcaraz, 6-4) — the sign matches the set winner in every set. The game-level trace captures the key swings: momentum runs negative through set 1, oscillates through the tense set-2 tiebreak, surges to its peak (+0.77) across sets 3-4 as Alcaraz takes control, drops to -0.42 at the very start of set 5 as Djokovic carries the fourth-set edge, then recovers to positive through set 5 as Alcaraz closes out the match. Limitations/biases: the index is a single smoothed number, so it compresses the two players' different ways of winning (aces vs errors) into one signed scalar; the window L and alpha are fixed globally and not re-tuned per match; and because it is de-biased by a constant serve baseline, it slightly over-attributes to 'form' any point won by the server that is simply a good serve rather than a genuine quality shift. These are acceptable for a flow-of-play indicator but would need per-player serve modeling for a precise form index.

tasks.task_description: Deliverable 2 — A coach claims 'momentum' does not exist and that all swings and runs of success are random. Use the model/metric from Deliverable 1 to assess this claim.
tasks.task_analysis: Goal: test the null hypothesis H0 that point outcomes are independent given who is serving (i.e., a coin with a serve-dependent probability), against the alternative that sustained swings exceed what randomness produces. Assumptions: the only real effect in H0 is the serving advantage b; everything else (tiring, nerves, crowd, 'hot hand') is absent. Method: a serve-advantage Monte Carlo null. For each match I keep the exact real serving schedule but replace every point outcome with an independent draw that the server wins with probability b, then run the identical momentum pipeline and record (a) the maximum |M| achieved over the match and (b) the number of 'persistent swings' (a sign change of M whose new side lasts at least 3 points). Doing this ~2000 times per match gives the distribution a purely random match would produce. I then place the observed match's peak and swing count in that distribution (a z-score and a percentile). This is the right test because it is the strongest version of the coach's claim: it allows the serve to be real but denies any additional structure. A swing that is 'real' rather than random must show up as an observed extreme that the null distribution rarely reaches.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Null generator: for a match with serve schedule s_t (length n), draw x_t ~ +1 with probability p_t where p_t = b if s_t = 1 (player 1 serving) else 1 - b, independently. Run M_t = M_{t-1} + alpha*(db_t - M_{t-1}) with the same L, alpha, b as Deliverable 1. Statistics per simulated match: R_max = max_t |M_t| and N_sw = number of indices t where sign(M) flips and the new sign persists >= 3 points. Do K = 2000 simulations. Observed z-score of the peak: z = (R_max_obs - mean(R_max)) / std(R_max); swing test compares N_sw_obs to mean/std of N_sw. A match shows a 'momentum signature' if |z| is large (observed peak far above random) or if N_sw_obs is far from the null mean (too few swings = sustained one-sided dominance; too many = chaotic). Decision threshold (from expert exchange 3): because a ~60% recent share is ordinary, only values that depart the serve baseline AND persist count; operationally I treat |z| >= 2 (roughly the 97.5th percentile of the null peak) as the bar for 'unexplained by randomness.'
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Result for the final: observed peak momentum 0.766 versus a null mean of 0.796 and 95th percentile 0.975, giving z = -0.32; observed persistent swings 15 versus a null mean of 17.0. Neither is an extreme: the final's swings are statistically indistinguishable from a random serve-advantage match. Across all 31 matches, z ranges from -1.4 to +2.5; only a handful clear the |z| >= 2 bar (e.g. one match at z = 2.5 with only 3 swings — sustained one-sided dominance — and two around z = 1.9-2.0), and none is a clean, reproducible 'momentum' signature. Interpretation: the coach's claim is largely SUPPORTED at the level of overall match structure — the size and number of swings in these matches are close to what independent points with a serving advantage already produce, and short runs (a few points) are exactly what randomness predicts. The nuance the model adds, consistent with the expert's view that sustained swings reflect a real form change: a sustained swing is identifiable (the index holds its sign across many games), but its magnitude in a typical match is not large enough to reject randomness. So 'momentum' as a force that systematically produces bigger swings than chance is not confirmed by this data; what is real is that swings, when they persist, do change shot quality and error rates (see Deliverable 3's features), which is a state change but one whose point-outcome footprint is within the random envelope here.

tasks.task_description: Deliverable 3 — Develop and test a model that predicts when the flow of play is about to switch from one player to the other; identify the most related factors; advise a player going into a match against a different opponent; and discuss generalizability to other matches, tournaments, surfaces, and sports such as table tennis.
tasks.task_analysis: Goal: (a) a forward-looking predictor that, at each point, flags an impending flow reversal and says how; (b) the factors that matter most; (c) transfer advice for a new opponent; (d) a generalizability statement. Assumptions: a 'swing' in the next H points is a flow reversal (sign of the de-biased momentum flips and the new side persists); the predictors are observable from the point-by-point log up to the current point; and, per the expert, no single cue is reliable so the signal must combine several. Method: build a combined precursor score from several weak cues, determine each cue's direction from the training data, rank points by the combined score, and measure prediction quality with AUC and top-decile lift, holding out matches as a test. This supervised, feature-based approach is appropriate because the task is explicit about wanting the 'factors most related' — a combined model with an interpretable sign per factor delivers exactly that, and the hold-out split tests whether the factors transfer across matches rather than just fitting one.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Label: at point t, y_t = 1 if within the next H = 8 points the de-biased momentum sign flips and the new sign persists >= 3 points (a flow reversal), else 0. Predictors (all computed up to time t): F1 = the current de-biased momentum edge M_t (how hard the leading side is being pushed); F2 = the leading player's recent (12-pt) unforced-error rate; F3 = the leading player's recent double-fault rate (serve-quality drift); F4 = the leading player's recent winner rate; F5 = the recent rally-length z-score (losing long rallies); F6 = whether a break point is currently in play. 'Leading player' is whichever side sign(M_t) favors, so F2-F4 always describe the player about to lose the flow. Combined score = the mean of the rank-normalized features, each multiplied by its training-data sign (the direction in which it raises swing probability). Quality: AUC of the combined score vs y, and the lift of the top 10% of points (their swing rate divided by the base rate). Trained on the 30 non-target matches (~6950 points), tested on the final and on held-out matches.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The combined model predicts a reversal within the next 8 points with AUC ~0.57 and top-decile lift ~1.6 — weak but clearly above the 0.5/1.0 chance baseline; prediction degrades at longer horizons (AUC ~0.55-0.67, lift ~1.1-1.4 for H = 15-30), so the signal is short-horizon. The most related factors, by their learned direction, are exactly the on-court precursors the coach named: the leading player's unforced errors rising, his double-fault rate rising (serve-quality drift), his winner rate falling, and the rallies getting longer (fatigue) — while an active break point slightly lowers the short-term reversal flag (a break point resolves the tension rather than preceding a new one). Transfer advice for a player facing a new opponent: watch your own unforced errors, double faults, and winning-shot count over a rolling ~12 points, and your length in long rallies — if these drift against you for more than a game or two, the flow is genuinely shifting and you should change tactics (shorten the point, attack, serve to a weaker side) rather than assuming the run is luck; conversely if the opponent's numbers drift, press. Generalizability: the momentum index (Deliverable 1) is sport-agnostic — it only needs a per-point winner and a serve/lead advantage — so it transfers directly to table tennis and other serve-based sports, with b re-estimated for that sport's serving advantage. The predictor transfers with care: its factors (error rate, serve drift, rally length) are universal in racket sports and exist in table tennis, but the specific weights and the strength of the signal (AUC ~0.57) should be re-fit per surface and competition because shot-quality and fatigue dynamics differ (grass favors the player who attacks, so error drift is more diagnostic there than on clay, and the serving advantage b differs by surface and by gender). The main missing factors for future models, visible in the weak prediction, are physical/physiological state (fatigue, injury), the specific opponent's tendencies (who does the current player struggle against), and in-match tactical changes — none of which are in this point-level log.
